name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: An AI Gateway and Python SDK for Multi-Provider LLM Access
answer: LiteLLM is an AI gateway and Python library from BerriAI that calls over 100 LLM APIs in OpenAI or native format, adding cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging. It sits between your application and providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure, and Vertex AI, and is moving to a Rust core for lower latency and memory. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its own incident reports document production outages and silent cost regressions tied to specific versions, so version pinning and upgrade discipline matter.

sections.body: LiteLLM is made by BerriAI and published at github.com/BerriAI/litellm under a custom licence, with Python as its language and a last push dated October 3, 2026. It is two things at once: a Python SDK you import into your own code, and a proxy server, often called the LiteLLM AI Gateway, that sits between your applications and model providers. In the AI stack it occupies the gateway layer, the point through which model traffic passes, so it handles routing, authentication, budgets, rate limits, logging, and cost attribution rather than model training itself. The site describes it as the fastest, litest AI Gateway, with a Rust core and Python SDK, and says the project is moving to Rust with a commitment to sub-1ms overhead and a sub-100MB binary.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs are calling many providers through one interface, tracking spend per key, team, agent, or customer, enforcing budgets and TPM or RPM limits, load balancing and retrying across model groups, caching responses in Redis, and logging requests. The site also documents an Agent Gateway and an MCP Gateway, so it can authenticate callers of shared agents, forward verified user and team identity as headers, and centralize tool access and upstream OAuth credentials. It is strongest where a platform team needs one control plane over many providers and many internal consumers, and where per-user attribution of agent spend matters. The site's own benchmark claims the Rust gateway has the lowest p99 added latency and smallest memory footprint among the gateways tested, though that comparison is the vendor's own.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The Python SDK is approachable for anyone who has called an LLM API, since the point is to keep the OpenAI-style call shape while swapping providers. The gateway is a different level of work: running a proxy, configuring keys and teams, connecting Redis, and understanding budgets and routing rules assumes some backend and operations knowledge. The official site is documentation rather than a course, and it offers tutorials, for example on reliability testing multiple providers with batch_completion_models_all_responses and load_test_model, plus blog posts on gateway identity and FinOps. Those tutorials are candid about rough edges, noting that load_test_model returns a calls_made field that is always 100 whatever num_calls is, and that it has no interval or duration options, so you loop over it yourself. No mathematics beyond basic statistics is needed for the gateway work, though evaluating model quality is a separate skill.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The repository has about 60,090 stars, which indicates a large and active user base. The site lists integrations with Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, Vertex AI, vLLM, and Nvidia NIM among the providers it fronts, and it documents an A2A JSON-RPC interface for invoking shared agents, OIDC authentication, OAuth2 with authorization code and PKCE for MCP servers, and an Admin UI where agents appear with status and spend. Documentation is extensive, with 60 pages read, covering tutorials, gateway identity, incident reports, and release notes. The blog carries tags for ai-gateway and incident-report, and the incident posts are unusually detailed about root causes and version ranges. Community support beyond the docs is not described in the material reviewed, so the documentation and repository are the main channels the site itself evidences.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: LiteLLM serves both ends. The Python SDK is built for quick experiments, since you can point the same call at different providers with minimal changes, and the batch and load testing helpers are aimed at early reliability checks. The gateway is explicitly built for production, with SSO and SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management, and guardrails. The cost of that dual role is visible in the site's own numbers: the Python proxy peaks around 359MB of memory under load, and the Rust gateway is claimed to serve about 15x the throughput on about 11x less memory, cutting per-request overhead from about 7.5ms to about 0.05ms. The Rust gateway was an early beta at the time of writing, so the performance story is partly a promise about a migration still in progress rather than a settled property of the current release.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The star count and the enterprise features, including SSO, audit logs, and multi-team spend management, indicate real production use, and the incident reports describe enterprise customers running the proxy behind nginx in Kubernetes. That makes it a current choice rather than a legacy one, and the move to Rust suggests the project intends to stay current. For someone choosing what to learn, gateway skills transfer: routing, budgets, identity propagation, and cost attribution are the same problems whichever gateway you use. The material reviewed does not name specific adopting companies or give market share, so claims about how widely it is used in any particular industry would go beyond what the facts and the site support.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is a Python project with a Rust core, and it is typically used alongside whatever language your application is written in, since the gateway speaks HTTP and the SDK is one client among several. It sits in front of provider SDKs rather than replacing them, and the site notes it calls Mistral's API directly over HTTP via httpx and does not import the mistralai Python SDK anywhere in the codebase. It also fronts serving stacks such as vLLM and Nvidia NIM, so it can sit in front of self-hosted inference as well as hosted APIs. The polyglot pattern is a thin gateway in front of many backends, with the application talking to one endpoint and the gateway translating to each provider's native format.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site's own incident reports are the clearest statement of weakness. A Medium severity incident in v1.100.0 caused kernel OOM kills, one worker reaching 61GB RSS, and thousands of 502s and tens of thousands of 499s, requiring an unreachable Redis and a failing provider at the same time. A separate Medium severity incident in v1.91.0 and v1.91.1 silently broke Anthropic prompt caching for Claude Code on Bedrock, dropping cache hit rates from roughly 90% to 25-45% and raising daily spend 2-3x with no error surfaced. The Rust gateway was an early beta, and the site says the migration will eventually yield a pure Rust server serving 100% of traffic, which is not yet the case. The material reviewed does not settle long-term support windows, the full licence terms behind the custom licence, or independent benchmarks of the gateway claims.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
